clue.text: The Army's domestic task force?

blocks.note: surface reading: a military unit sent on duty at home rather than abroad
setter's reading: housework chores, the cleaning and cooking jobs soldiers are detailed to do in camp

explanation.surface: A military detachment posted to keep order on home soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Domestic' suggests home defence, but it means housework: fatigues are the menial chores given to soldiers, and a FATIGUE PARTY is the squad doing them.
explanation.definitionFit: In army slang fatigues are cleaning and cooking chores, and a party is a small group detailed together to carry them out.

clue.text: Easy to make crumble - can be cooked in fat?

blocks.note: first meaning: crumbly, readily broken into small pieces
second meaning, a pun: able to be fried, read as fry-able

explanation.surface: A kitchen note on a crumbly topping and whether it can go in the pan.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: the word is split as if it meant fit for the frying pan.
explanation.definitionFit: Friable soil or rock breaks up readily into crumbs; jokingly, the word looks like something suitable for frying.

clue.text: Peg to hold opera hat

indicators.note: to hold means to keep within, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: a golf tee is the small peg the ball sits on
op is the abbreviation for opus or opera, a musical work

explanation.surface: A hook in the cloakroom for hanging a collapsible opera hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opera hat' looks like one phrase, but the hat is the definition and opera only gives OP.
explanation.definitionFit: A topee is a lightweight sun helmet made of pith, worn in hot countries.

clue.text: Diverge, oddly, about a French verbal adjective

indicators.note: oddly means in a strange way, so the word just before it is rearranged
about means around, so the rearranged letters surround what follows

blocks.note: taken as written
un is the French for a

explanation.surface: A grammar puzzle: a French adjective formed from a verb strangely departs from the rule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' might suggest taking odd letters, but here it signals a shuffle of the whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin grammar the gerundive is a verb form used as an adjective, expressing what must be done.

clue.text: Old wives' kisses, say

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the symbols aloud and spell what we hear

blocks.note: kisses are written as Xs at the foot of a letter, and the letter X is pronounced ex

explanation.surface: Former wives remember the kisses they once received.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, the plural of the letter X is spelled out as EXES.
explanation.definitionFit: An ex is a former spouse or partner, so old wives are exes.

clue.text: Sort of betting before and after the event in Rome

blocks.note: ante is Latin for before
post is Latin for after, and in Rome tells us to use Latin

explanation.surface: Odds offered both ahead of and following a contest in the Italian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Ante-post betting is on a horse race placed well before the day, when odds are longer; in Rome tells us to put before and after into Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: Ante-post wagers are placed in advance of the final declarations for a race, at long odds.

clue.text: School crocodile

blocks.note: first meaning, a verb: to teach or coach
second meaning: a long line of people walking one behind another

explanation.walkthrough: A crocodile is the British term for schoolchildren walking in pairs in a line, so the surface suggests a single school outing.
explanation.definitionFit: To school is to instruct or drill, and a crocodile of walkers forms a long procession or line.

clue.text: Girl admits forged coin is a plant

indicators.note: forged means faked or hammered into shape, so its neighbour is rearranged
admits means lets in, so the first piece takes the rest inside

blocks.note: Vera is a girl's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl confesses that a counterfeit coin is a planted piece of evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like the criminal sense, something planted to frame someone, but it is the botanical one.
explanation.definitionFit: Veronica, or speedwell, is a flowering garden plant with small blue flowers.

clue.text: Restaurant proprietor who might give someone a living

definitions.text: who might give someone a living

blocks.note: first meaning: the French word for the owner of a cafe or restaurant

blocks.clueFragment: who might give someone a living
blocks.note: second meaning: one who holds the right to appoint a clergyman to a church benefice

explanation.walkthrough: A living is a Church of England benefice, a parish post with income, and its patron chooses the vicar.
explanation.definitionFit: The owner of a French bistro is called le patron, and a patron of a parish has the right to present its priest.

clue.text: One male ideal that is not fully realized

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
the standard abbreviation for male
ideal and perfect are synonyms, both meaning flawless

explanation.surface: A man's dream that never quite comes true.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flawed or incomplete falls short of being achieved; in grammar the imperfect tense describes an action still unfinished.

clue.text: Return a cycle to the sports ground

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the words that follow are read from the end to the start

blocks.note: a cycle is an era, a recurring age or period

explanation.surface: Bring a bicycle back to the stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A cycle' looks like a bike, but here it is AN ERA, a period of time; written backwards it gives ARENA.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is an enclosed space where sports events and contests are staged before spectators.

clue.text: Rachel's little boy catching lake fish

indicators.note: catching means taking hold of, so the first piece wraps around the next

blocks.note: in Genesis Rachel's younger son is Benjamin, and Benny is his pet name
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A small boy out angling hooks something from the lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bible supplies the boy: Rachel was the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, so her little boy is BENNY, with L inside giving BLENNY.
explanation.definitionFit: Blennies are small spiny-finned fish of rock pools and shallow coastal waters.

clue.text: No point knocking here the tradesman's entrance is free

definitions.text: No point knocking here the tradesman's entrance is free

blocks.clueFragment: No point knocking here the tradesman's entrance is free
blocks.note: surface reading: a delivery man finds the back door unlocked and walks straight in
setter's reading: free access for trade, a policy of letting all merchants in on equal terms

explanation.surface: A delivery man finds no need to knock, since the back door is unlocked.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is a literal unlatched door; the phrase also names the trade policy of admitting all foreign merchants freely.
explanation.definitionFit: An unlatched entrance needs no knock, and the same phrase names a policy of unrestricted access for traders, as in China's treaty ports.

clue.text: Optical shutter

blocks.note: surface reading: the shutter in a camera or optical instrument
setter's reading: the fold of skin that closes over the eye

explanation.walkthrough: The words suggest camera equipment, but the shutter belongs to the body and closes over the eye when we blink.
explanation.definitionFit: The movable skin fold over each eye closes it like a camera shutter, blocking light during sleep or a blink.

clue.text: The total number of sappers in existence

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the troops go within what follows

blocks.note: entity means being or existence
the Royal Engineers, the corps of sappers in the British Army

explanation.surface: A head count of all the army engineers still alive.
explanation.walkthrough: Sappers are military engineers, and RE, the Royal Engineers, is the crossword shorthand for them.
explanation.definitionFit: The entirety of something is the whole of it, everything taken together.

clue.text: Mishit an error in these games

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective naming these games, the Isthmian Games

indicators.note: an error puts things wrong, so the letters before it come out in a muddled order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sportsman blames a mistimed stroke for a mistake during the tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isthmian Games were athletic contests held at Corinth, on the narrow neck of land joining the Peloponnese to mainland Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek festival on the Corinthian isthmus was called the Isthmian Games, so the adjective names them.

clue.text: Church girl rings twice - a variation of telling the hours

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the adjective, about measuring time

indicators.note: a variation is an altered form, so the preceding letters are rearranged

blocks.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
taken as written
a ring is shaped like the letter O; read as rings, plural, and then two more, the setter wants three

explanation.surface: A girl at church rings the bells over and over to mark the hours.
explanation.walkthrough: The ring count is loose: the answer needs three Os, so 'rings twice' has to supply three rather than the two a strict reading gives.
explanation.definitionFit: Horologic relates to horology, the science of measuring time and making clocks and watches.

clue.text: 1000 to one race is an error

blocks.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
I is the Roman numeral for one
a sprint is a short fast race

explanation.surface: Betting a thousand to one on a race is a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: '1000 to one' reads as betting odds, but it is two Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: A misprint is a typographical mistake in printed text.

clue.text: Inadequate parking - he's in the top storey

indicators.note: in places the word just before it inside the phrase that follows

blocks.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
the attic is the room at the top of a house, under the roof
taken as written, from he's, read as he is

explanation.surface: A driver complains that the multi-storey's only spaces are up on the roof level.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the apostrophe in he's as 'he is', so the pronoun sits within the top room rather than owning it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathetic in its casual sense means feeble or woefully poor, which is what an inadequate effort is.

clue.text: With father, the beginning and end of charity is a religious organisation

indicators.note: the beginning and end of a word are its first and last letters only

blocks.note: papa is a child's word for father
the first and last letters of charity

explanation.surface: Together with a priest, charity starts and ends a church body.
explanation.definitionFit: The papacy is the office of the Pope and, by extension, the governing system of the Roman Catholic Church.

clue.text: Don't start to criticise the fire-water!

indicators.note: told not to start, the word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: to barrack is to jeer at and heckle, especially from a crowd

explanation.surface: A warning against condemning someone's strong drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Barrack is British and Australian usage for heckling performers or players; drop its B to leave the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrack is a strong spirit distilled in Asia from palm sap or rice, the kind of liquor nicknamed fire-water.

clue.text: Lively party, where Mrs Brown was invited to dance?

definitions.text: where Mrs Brown was invited to dance?

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for a boisterous get-together with singing and dancing

blocks.clueFragment: where Mrs Brown was invited to dance?
blocks.note: second meaning: the music-hall song whose chorus urges Mother Brown to kick up her legs

explanation.surface: A rowdy party where a middle-aged lady was asked onto the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Knees Up Mother Brown is an old London music-hall singalong; a knees-up is British slang for a lively party.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowdy celebration with singing and dancing is a knees-up, from the high-kicking dance in the song.

clue.text: Short passage from satirist about a schoolboy

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: Alexander Pope, the eighteenth-century satirical poet
Eric, or Little by Little is a Victorian school story, so Eric stands for a schoolboy

explanation.surface: An extract from a satirical writer poking fun at a pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric, or Little by Little (1858) was a famous moralising school story, which is why setters use Eric for any schoolboy.
explanation.definitionFit: A pericope is a short extract from a text, especially a Bible reading set for a church service.

clue.text: He has the remedy for a smoker

definitions.text: He has the remedy for a smoker

blocks.clueFragment: He has the remedy for a smoker
blocks.note: surface reading: a doctor or therapist who helps people give up cigarettes
setter's reading: one who preserves fish or meat by salting and smoking, the smokehouse trade

explanation.surface: A therapist claims he can help anyone quit tobacco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoker' suggests a cigarette habit, but it is the smoking of fish and bacon, done by someone who preserves them.
explanation.definitionFit: One who heals sickness is called this, and so is the tradesman who preserves bacon or fish by salting and smoking.

clue.text: Left in peace, say, he is full of joy

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the previous word and take a different word with that sound
in places the word before it inside the following piece

blocks.note: peace sounds like piece, and a piece is a bit
L is the standard abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone left undisturbed is cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left in peace' reads as one phrase meaning undisturbed, but Left is just the letter and peace is heard as its sound-alike piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Blithe means carefree and cheerful, happily untroubled.

clue.text: In absentia, ranked as top band

indicators.note: In tells us the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: letters spanning the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A musical group voted best in the charts without being present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top band' suggests a chart-topping group, but it is a band worn on top of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled ornamental circlet worn on the head.

clue.text: This is the platform for departures, the porter said

definitions.text: This is the platform for departures

indicators.note: said asks us to take the word as it is spoken, not as written

blocks.note: porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: A railway porter tells a traveller which platform the trains leave from.
explanation.walkthrough: The departed here are the dead, and porter is also a kind of dark beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bier is the stand on which a coffin or corpse is placed before burial, so it carries the departed.

clue.text: Provide food in battered crate

indicators.note: something battered is knocked out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Supplies of food delivered in a damaged box.
explanation.definitionFit: To cater is to supply meals and refreshments, as for a party or function.

clue.text: Silas in G & S version used to make jellies

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun

indicators.note: a version is a rendering in another form, so the letters are recast

blocks.note: taken as written, the ampersand adding nothing

explanation.surface: A Gilbert and Sullivan adaptation featuring a character named Silas.
explanation.walkthrough: G & S is Gilbert and Sullivan, the Victorian comic opera partnership, but here only the letters G and S count.
explanation.definitionFit: Isinglass is a pure gelatin obtained from fish bladders, traditionally used for setting jellies and clarifying beer.

clue.text: Author's contraction avoided in typing

blocks.note: surface reading: a shortened word or abbreviation an author uses
setter's reading: a muscle spasm of the hand from long hours with a pen, which a typist escapes

explanation.surface: A writer's abbreviation that doesn't get used when the text is typed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contraction' looks grammatical, like don't for do not, but it is a muscle cramping in the hand that holds the pen.
explanation.definitionFit: The painful hand spasm brought on by prolonged handwriting is named for those who write most.
